title: How Often Should You Restain Your Deck? A Practical Guide
metaTitle: How Often to Restain a Deck | Ontario Timeline Guide
metaDescription: Product type, prep quality and Ontario's climate all affect how long deck stain lasts. Here is how to tell when it's actually time to restain, not just guess.
excerpt: The calendar is only a starting point. Here is how to read your own deck's condition, understand what Ontario's climate does to stain, and know exactly when it's time to restain rather than wait another season.
heroAlt: Water beading on freshly stained deck boards versus soaking into unprotected weathered wood nearby
keyTakeaways: Premium penetrating oil-based stains like Ready Seal and Penofin Verde typically need maintenance re-staining every 2 to 4 years, with a full restoration every 5 to 7 years.
The water bead test is the single fastest way to check whether your stain is still protecting the deck: if water soaks in instead of beading, it's time to book restoration.
Greying wood, uneven fading, mold or algae growth, and peeling or bubbling are the four visual warning signs to check every spring, in roughly that order of severity.
Ontario's 40-plus annual freeze-thaw cycles, high summer UV and heavy snow loading all shorten stain life compared to milder climates.
Waiting past the ideal restaining window doesn't just risk a worse-looking deck, it steadily increases the cost of the eventual restoration.

body.text: One of the most common questions homeowners ask us is some version of "how do I know when my deck actually needs to be restained?" There isn't a single fixed number of years that applies to every deck, because the answer depends on the product originally used, how thoroughly the deck was prepped before that stain went on, how much sun and rain the deck sees, and Ontario's climate specifically. What follows is a practical way to think about timing, plus the visual signs that tell you more than any calendar can.
General timelines by product type

As a starting point, here are typical maintenance intervals for well-applied stain on a properly prepped deck in this region. A premium penetrating oil-based stain, such as Ready Seal or Penofin Verde, generally needs a full restoration every 5 to 7 years, with lighter maintenance re-staining every 2 to 4 years in between. Standard oil-based stain without the same premium formulation tends to need restaining every 2 to 3 years. Water-based or latex stain typically runs 1 to 3 years depending on product quality and how well the deck was prepped beforehand. A clear sealant with no pigment offers the shortest protection window, usually 1 to 2 years, since it provides less UV resistance and breaks down faster under direct sun.

items: Premium penetrating oil-based stain (Ready Seal, Penofin Verde): full restoration every 5 to 7 years, maintenance re-stain every 2 to 4 years
Standard oil-based stain: re-stain every 2 to 3 years
Water-based / latex stain: 1 to 3 years depending on product and prep quality
Clear sealant only, no pigment: every 1 to 2 years due to weaker UV protection

body.text: These are rough guides, not guarantees. A deck in full afternoon sun will wear faster than one shaded by mature trees, and a deck that was properly prepped before its last stain job will hold up longer than one that wasn't. The actual condition of your deck always matters more than the number of years since the last coat.
Warning signs it's time to restain

Rather than waiting for the wood to visibly deteriorate, check for these signs every spring. Catching them early is the difference between a routine maintenance re-stain and a much larger repair bill down the line.
1. Water no longer beads on the surface

Splash a cup of water on the deck. If it beads up and sits on the surface for several seconds, the stain is still doing its job. If it soaks in immediately and darkens the wood, the protective barrier has broken down. Unprotected wood absorbs moisture with every rainfall, and that absorbed moisture is what eventually leads to mold, swelling and rot.
2. The wood has turned grey or silver

That grey colour isn't just cosmetic, it's UV radiation breaking down the lignin that binds wood fibres together. The greying signals the wood is aging and drying out without protection. The good news is that grey decks are almost always restorable with a thorough professional clean and a fresh stain coat, provided you act before the degradation reaches deeper into the wood.
3. The stain is fading unevenly

Patchy, uneven fading means some areas of the deck have lost their protection faster than others. South-facing boards, spots that get intense afternoon sun, and high-traffic walking paths typically fade first. Once entire sections look noticeably lighter or more weathered than the rest of the deck, it's a clear signal that a full refresh is due.
4. Mold or algae appearing on the surface

Black staining, green patches or fuzzy growth mean moisture is sitting in or on the wood longer than it should. Mold appearing on a stained deck means the stain's biocide protection has expired. Left untreated, some mold species produce enzymes that actively accelerate wood decay, so this sign shouldn't wait for a convenient weekend.
5. Peeling, flaking or bubbling

This is the most serious sign and typically points to a film-forming finish, paint or solid stain, that has failed outright. Bubbling usually means moisture got trapped under the film before it fully cured, and peeling means the bond between the finish and the wood has broken. Either way, the existing finish has to be fully stripped before any new product goes on; you cannot stain over a peeling deck and expect it to hold.
Do the water bead test every spring, after the last freeze-thaw cycle and before summer use begins. It takes ten seconds and tells you more than guessing from the calendar ever will.
How Ontario's climate shortens stain life

Compared to milder climates, decks in this region face a harder set of conditions. There are 40 or more freeze-thaw cycles in a typical year, and each one stresses wood fibres and any film-forming finish sitting on top as water expands inside cracks and pores. High summer UV breaks down both the pigment, causing visible fading, and the protective compounds within the stain itself. Spring rain and humidity promote mold and algae growth, particularly on shaded, north-facing decks that don't get enough sun to dry out between rainfalls. And heavy snow sitting on a deck for months at a time keeps moisture in continuous contact with the wood through the coldest part of the year. This combination is exactly why we recommend premium penetrating oil-based stains for decks in this climate: they move with the wood through seasonal swings rather than forming a brittle surface film that eventually cracks under the strain. See /oil-based-vs-water-based-deck-stain for the full comparison.
The cost of waiting too long

The longer a deck goes past its ideal maintenance window, the more work, and cost, the eventual restoration requires. On-time maintenance, a clean, light sand and restain, typically runs $800 to $1,500. An overdue deck showing greying and some early peeling usually needs a deeper clean, repairs to a handful of boards, a full sand and restain, running $1,200 to $2,000. A genuinely neglected deck with significant rot and extensive peeling requires board replacement layered on top of a full restoration, generally $2,000 to $3,500 or more. And a structurally compromised deck, where the frame itself has been affected, can require a partial or full rebuild running $8,000 to $40,000 or beyond. Staying on a regular 2 to 4 year maintenance cycle with a quality oil-based product is consistently the most cost-effective approach over the life of a deck. More detail on that trade-off is covered in /how-to-save-money-restore-dont-replace.
Our recommendation

Inspect your deck every spring, after the last freeze-thaw cycle and before it sees heavy summer use. Run the water bead test, and if water soaks in rather than beading, book your restoration before summer arrives rather than waiting for the wood to visibly deteriorate. A deck that goes into winter properly protected holds up far better against freeze-thaw cycles than one facing them with bare, unprotected wood. faq.q: How often should I restain my deck in Ontario?
faq.a: With a premium penetrating oil-based stain like Ready Seal or Penofin Verde, expect a maintenance re-stain every 2 to 4 years and a full restoration every 5 to 7 years. Standard oil-based products run closer to every 2 to 3 years, and water-based products every 1 to 3 years.

faq.q: What is the water bead test and how do I do it?
faq.a: Splash a cup of water on the deck surface. If it beads up and sits for several seconds, the stain is still protecting the wood. If it soaks in immediately and darkens the boards, the protective barrier has broken down and it's time to restain.

faq.q: Does grey wood always mean I need to restain right away?
faq.a: Grey colouration means UV has broken down the surface wood fibres, which does signal the finish has worn away, but it's usually still fully restorable with a professional clean, light sand and fresh stain, provided you act before the degradation goes deeper.

faq.q: Why does Ontario's climate wear out deck stain faster than other regions?
faq.a: This region sees 40 or more freeze-thaw cycles per year plus high summer UV and heavy winter snow loading, all of which stress wood fibres and any protective finish more aggressively than milder climates experience.

faq.q: What happens if I wait too long to restain my deck?
faq.a: Costs rise steadily the longer you wait. On-time maintenance runs $800 to $1,500, an overdue deck with some peeling runs $1,200 to $2,000, and a neglected deck with rot and extensive peeling can run $2,000 to $3,500 or more before any structural repair is needed.

faq.q: Can I stain over a peeling or bubbling deck?
faq.a: No. Peeling or bubbling means the existing finish has failed and must be fully stripped or sanded back to bare wood before any new stain is applied. Staining over a failing finish will fail at the same rate almost immediately.
